$comment: A ROUTINE RUN NEVER YIELDS. Run No.61 stopped three times on permission
prompts for ordinary file writes, and a stop is indistinguishable from
asking a human who is not there. Everything this routine does every single
run is allowlisted here so the run cannot be halted by its own plumbing.
THIS FILE IS TRACKED, AND THAT IS THE POINT. The rules lived briefly in a
gitignored .claude/settings.local.json, which was worse than useless: this
routine runs in a FRESH CONTAINER every day, cloned from the repo, so a file
that is never committed does not exist on the run that needs it. The stops
would have come back tomorrow and the deny list would have protected
nothing. Enforceable rules belong in tracked configuration.
READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING THE ALLOW LIST. It is NOT a sandbox and not a
security boundary. Bash, and Bash(python3:*) in particular, runs anything:
python3 -c can rewrite a ledger, delete runs/, drive git, or reach the
network, straight past every narrower Write and Edit rule here. An earlier
version of this comment claimed the opposite. That claim was false, and a
false safeguard is worse than none.
THESE ROUTINES DRAFT ONLY AND NEVER SEND, and that is now enforced rather
than merely written down: the Gmail send, forward and reply tools are in the
deny list, along with trashing a message or a thread. create_draft and
update_draft stay allowed, because drafting is the job. CLAUDE.md has said
'never send' since the first run; a rule the harness checks is worth more
than a rule the model has to remember at three in the morning.
WHAT THE DENY LIST DOES AND DOES NOT REACH. Tool-level denies (the Gmail
send, forward and reply entries above) are solid: there is no other tool
that sends, and Bash has no credentials for one. The PATH denies are weaker
than they look, and an earlier version of this comment oversold them. Bash
is allowed, and a heredoc or `python3 -c` or `sed -i` reaches a path without
ever consulting a Write or Edit rule, so the ledger denies below are a
seatbelt and not a lock.
The LOCK for the cron-written ledgers is scripts/ledger_guard.py, which is a
row in gate_status.py. It compares the shipped diff against the base branch
and FAILS the run if any of those files moved, which catches the write
however it was made and in time to stop the merge. That is the pattern to
copy whenever a rule here needs to be a guarantee: state it in the deny list
for the easy cases, and enforce it in a check that runs on the artifact.
The same caution applies to the local mirror. bootstrap.sh copies this file
to .claude/settings.local.json, which helps once a session is running, but
it CANNOT rescue the very first tool call: running bootstrap is itself a
Bash call that the project rules have to permit. The thing that actually
removed the recurring stop was moving the worklog out of .claude/ and into
out/, so the sensitive write stopped happening at all.
Everything else that matters (a push, a merge, deleting under runs/) is
protected by the rules in CLAUDE.md and by guards written into the scripts,
where they can be tested: see scripts/wrap_run.py, which refuses any path
under runs/ that is not the two files it owns.
effortLevel, 2026-09-23. The routine moved to a model whose Claude Code
default effort is medium, one level below the high the previous model
defaulted to, and a scheduled run passes no effort of its own (the September
19th and 20th routine sessions record none). So this key is the level every
scheduled run reasons at, and every subagent inherits it unless its own
frontmatter names one. Anthropic's guidance for the new model: its medium
already matches or beats the previous model's high on coding and knowledge
work, it thinks more per turn at any given level, and xhigh and max are for
gains somebody has measured. high is one step above its default, more
reasoning than any earlier run had, at a lower price per token. Raise it on
evidence, never on a hunch: every routine on this account shares the same
usage limits. The routine records $CLAUDE_EFFORT in run_state.json at wake,
so every run says whether this line took.
